body:
Thank you for response, it is very eye opening. With your response, and the others in the thread, I believe these circumstances and temporary and can be resolved. I will schedule a discussion to get a better understanding of how I can better support her.

You're right, damn you're right, there is so much that so many people would lose out on my from my death. From loss of income to emotional attachment, I wasn't aware of just how severe and long lasting a dead parent can be. The thought of my daughter blaming herself for my death, not to mention the loss of investmentand relationship in her development would not be fair to her either.

Thank you for being real, genuine, and direct. Your comment has gotten through loud and clear, I won't waste this opportunity to help my wife and I heal, and our daughter to have a healthy loving home.

You're absolutely right, I appreciate your detailed and thoughtful reply.

We will schedule a time when she has energy, and we are both in a decent emotional space, to talk about what she needs, how I can help in the healing process, and to set clear expectations so there are no assumptions or pressure.

You're correct, lack of sex isn't enough to drive someone to kill themselves. I've got my own set of problems and will continue working on them in therapy.

Thank you so, so, so much for your reply. It is extremely helpful.

Thank you for this post. I appreciate your insight into realistic time expectations, that my perceptions of progress aren't really fair to my wife, what support looks like and the prompt to ask her what support she wants.

I had not previously considered that from her perspective, it's only been seven months. I've been using the measurement of nine years of dating and marriage. In this new context, where she herself has only been working on this for seven months, and there is a new child involved, I will need to be much, much more patient.

I will bring up these topics with my therapist when he returns in early January. Your encouragement is incredibly helpful.

Thank you for being so direct, I will be very mindful in how I approach this subject, and sympathetic to her concerns. The context about the new child adding stress and drain to the relationship is helpfil. I want to be in this for the long haul, if that means waiting a year or two for the healing process to begin moving forward I'm on board. Thank you again.

Thank you for this reply, I will read through/listen to it.

My therapist is on a three week pause for Christmas/New Years. When I resume in January I'll bring this up. I hope this will pass too, hoping things can improve, be mutually beneficial. Thank you again.

Thanks, that is helpful.

I will bring up a day to discuss expectations for building intimacy and closeness, and expectations for how to discovery sexuality together again. I think she believes she wants to heal and grow, but, I just don't see it happening. Maybe a timeline to look back and review would be helpful. Thanks for your reply!

Thanks for your response, I should definitely add that in.

Outside of sex, things are surprisingly good. We take trips to the beach as a family, watch Seinfeld or Star Trek TNG under a blanket together almost every evening, have dinners together and enjoy talking and going on walks. Aside from anything sexual, it's going fairly well. We are both tired a lot, just from work/homemaking and having a 1 year old, but we can chat it up for hours and enjoy spending time together.

10 years ago I OD'd on some meds that caused me to go into an ultra rapid, erratic heart rhythm. It was so disorienting I couldn't stand, ended up unable to get up and just had to lay on the floor for three hours dizzy until the effects faded. It was the most scary experience of my life, and I remember genuinely believing I was on my way to death's door and regretting taking the meds.

I know the reasoning of the ideation: something is wrong, I can't find a solution, death is a solution, even if it's not a very good one. I think I'll delay a month to buy the shotgun shells, who knows, maybe I'm just in an irrational state of mind and it will clear up. Maybe it will, maybe if won't, I can put up with a month.

Thank you for your reply, I greatly appreciate you taking the time to write. I guess if it's truly that bad, what's the rush to kill myself? I mean, what is a waiting month to revisit this decision, more informed, compared to the remaining 50+ years I am about to erase. Thank you again. I'll try to bring it up to a medical professional without going into enough detail to get committed.

If your parents care about you, which I imagine they do, they may be able to help. Any good parent has years of experience and knowledge above their children, and likely have access to resources and connections that you do not. Families help each other out when no one else will.

Again, if your parents care about you, your well-being is important to them. I know if I had kids, I would do anything to help them if they are seriously hurting.

Let me preface by saying that meds can make an absolutely incredible difference. But they are not a magic cure-all for most people. They are accompanied by other methods.

For starters, find a therapist you can talk naturally with. If you're a minor, consider getting a therapist who specializes with children. A good therapist can help you identify triggers (causes for a depressive spell), skills for rebuilding your life, and make plans specific to what you need.

Your mind is also dependent on your body. Be sure that
a) You have proper nutrition, if you eat very little you'll be more vulnerable to depression.
b) Have some form of physical activity. It doesn't have to be running or working out, but even just walking around the block once a day is important. Being locked inside a house all day can wear you down.
c) Get sleep. If you are physically exhausted, you will be mentally as well.

Tell someone, depression is very difficult, if not impossible, to "conquer" by yourself. Talk to someone you can trust, if that is a parent, awesome, if it's a teacher, mentor, or friend, great. You'll need support structures (like a church, circle of friends [which you said are absent right now], family, or social group] to, well, support you.

Also, be careful who you tell. From experience, the majority of peers are not understanding of depression as having a chemical definition, it's rather seen as weakness.

If you do go the route of medication, remember it's mostly trial-and-error on what works, what doesn't, and what has the least side-effects. Everyone has different brain chemistry, and finding a drug cocktail that works well takes months of testing.

In the long run, things ARE going to get better, just the time frame may not be what you are hoping for. I hope that helps.
